clean_text: #PokémonVGC #PokémonACS First of all, even until now, I still can’t fully believe that I’ve reached this stage. Everything feels like a dream to me. My very first milestone was simply to become a Malaysian representative at Worlds, but things happened so quickly that it still feels unreal. Not only am I representing my home country on the world stage, but I can now proudly say that I am officially the Pokémon Malaysia Asia Championship Master Ball League 2026 Champion. At 24 years old, many people would still consider me young and say that I have plenty of time ahead of me to chase my dreams. And yes, while Pokémon Champions has only been released for about a month, I’ve told many opponents and people I met during the event that I only started playing competitive VGC seriously after this game launched. However, I believe only my family truly understands how hard I’ve been pushing myself for the past 10 years to reach this moment. Some people may wonder why I keep mentioning “10 years” when I only recently started competitive Pokémon VGC. The reason is because my competitive journey didn’t begin with Pokémon. Over the years, I moved from game to game, constantly trying my best in every title where I believed I had potential. When I was 16, I even received an offer from a professional esports team to join them, earn a monthly salary, and represent both the team and Malaysia internationally. But after discussing it with my parents, I decided to reject the offer because academics felt like the safer and more important path for my future. That decision left a regret in my heart that stayed with me for the next 10 years. During college, I discovered another opportunity through Pokémon Unite. It was my first experience competing in a team-based game that required teamwork, communication, and trust to achieve victory together. From that moment onward, I spent almost every free hour outside of my studies practicing and improving. Balancing academics and my competitive dreams was never easy because both meant equally much to me. It has now been five years since Pokémon Unite was released, and while my teams and I managed to qualify for multiple Day 2 elimination stages, my best achievement so far has been finishing Top 8 at the Southeast Asia Championship. Even so, I’ve never given up on the game, and I’ll continue striving for better results together with my teammates in the upcoming World Championship. I may have gone a little too deep into my past, so let me return to the present. When Pokémon Champions was released, I knew the Malaysia Asia Championship was approaching quickly. In just one month, I had to catch up with players who already possessed over 10 years of VGC experience. While the game itself is new, competitive Pokémon has existed for over a decade, and Pokémon Champions simply became the newest platform for competitive play. For me, it was the perfect opportunity to finally step into this scene seriously from the beginning. One month ago, I couldn’t even imagine becoming the 2026 Malaysia Champion. I had to learn every meta Pokémon, understand base stats, memorize speed tiers, and adapt to competitive mechanics within an incredibly short time. It was a short journey in terms of time, but mentally it felt extremely long and exhausting because I was competing against players with years of experience over me. Because of that, I pressured myself constantly to improve. Every day after work, I spent hours practicing, studying streams from top players around the world, and learning as much as possible. I knew I had to work twice as hard just to keep up.
